_note: The root layer beneath the root layer: seven manuals and classifications that Canadian and US statistical agencies name in their own methodology documents, extending the two international nodes (sna-2008, icls-work-statistics-resolution) already in the graph. The shape of this slice is lopsided. NAICS is the hub — five of the eleven edges point at it, and it is the only standard both countries name for the same purpose, which makes it the strongest documented tie between the Canadian and US clusters after SNA 2008. The IMF manuals cluster tightly: a single StatCan page (13-607-X) declares that the Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts rests on exactly three frameworks — SNA 2008, BPM6 and the GFSM — so one document carries three edges. The lesson about evidence is that the national side almost always states the relationship more usefully than the international side, and that the giveaway phrasing is operational rather than declarative: agencies rarely write 'we conform to X', they write 'each establishment is assigned a code according to X' or footnote a specific design rule to a paragraph number in X. The weakest area is prices: neither agency treats the international CPI apparatus as governing. StatCan cites the CPI Manual but keeps its own basket classification; BLS explicitly disclaims NAICS for the CPI and produces COICOP only as a side output for the OECD.

reports.title: Consumer Price Index Manual: Concepts and Methods
reports.publisher: IMF, ILO, OECD, Eurostat, UNECE and the World Bank
reports.description: The internationally agreed manual of concepts, methods and practice for compiling a consumer price index. Jointly published by six international organisations and managed by the IMF; the 2020 edition updates the 2004 ILO-managed Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice. Country code is CA only because the schema offers no international option — the publisher is a consortium of international agencies.
reports.cadence_note: Revised roughly once a generation — editions in 1989, 2004 and 2020. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal so the pulse rate reads as near-static.

reports.title: North American Industry Classification System (NAICS)
reports.publisher: Statistics Canada, U.S. Office of Management and Budget / Economic Classification Policy Committee, and INEGI (Mexico)
reports.description: The trinational industry classification used to organise economic statistics in Canada, the United States and Mexico, using a six-digit hierarchical code. Agreed and revised jointly by the three countries' statistical agencies; each publishes its own national version (NAICS Canada, NAICS United States, SCIAN Mexico) from a common structure. It is the single classification most widely named across both countries' industry statistics.
reports.cadence_note: Revised on a five-year cycle — 1997, 2002, 2007, 2012, 2017, 2022. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal.

release_schedule.note: Still formally 'proposed' pending close of public comment as of the check date (Federal Register notice 2026-14086, published 2026-07-13 — exact document URL not resolved, worth a follow-up fetch). Standing rule is a 5-year review cycle.

reports.title: Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual, Sixth Edition (BPM6)
reports.description: The IMF's standard for compiling the balance of payments and the international investment position — the accounting framework for a country's transactions and positions with the rest of the world. Harmonised with SNA 2008. A seventh edition (BPM7) was developed alongside the 2025 SNA update. Country code is CA only because the schema offers no international option.
reports.cadence_note: Revised roughly once a generation — BPM5 in 1993, BPM6 in 2009. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal.

reports.title: Government Finance Statistics Manual (GFSM 2014)
reports.description: The IMF's standard framework for compiling statistics on the revenue, expense, financial position and financing of the general government and public sectors. Harmonised with SNA 2008 and BPM6, and the basis on which countries report comparable fiscal statistics. Country code is CA only because the schema offers no international option.
reports.cadence_note: Revised roughly once a generation — 1986, 2001, 2014. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal.

reports.title: International Public Sector Accounting Standards (IPSAS)
reports.publisher: International Public Sector Accounting Standards Board (IPSASB), IFAC
reports.description: The international accrual-basis accounting standards for governments and other public sector entities, issued by the IPSASB. Distinct from the statistical frameworks in this slice: IPSAS govern how a government's own financial statements are prepared rather than how national statistics are compiled. Country code is CA only because the schema offers no international option.
reports.cadence_note: The IPSASB issues new and amended standards on a rolling basis and publishes a consolidated Handbook annually.

entries.covers: IPSAS SRS 1 Climate Disclosures Phase 1 — approved

release_schedule.note: 10-entry dated project milestone list found; trimmed to 6 here for space (2 already past as of this audit, kept for context). Targets shift at each quarterly Board meeting — worth re-checking before relying on the later dates.

reports.title: Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses
reports.publisher: United Nations Statistics Division (Department of Economic and Social Affairs)
reports.description: The UN's standard guidance on planning, conducting and disseminating a population and housing census, including the characteristics of the population and housing that should be measured. Issued since 1958 and revised once each decennial census round to keep national censuses internationally comparable; Revision 3 covers the 2020 round and Revision 4 the 2030 round. Country code is CA only because the schema offers no international option.
reports.cadence_note: Revised once per decennial census round — roughly every ten years. Not an annual release; releases_per_year is nominal.

dependencies.basis: The Canadian Consumer Price Index Reference Paper (catalogue 62-553-X) Chapter 4 states the three criteria the CPI product and geographical classifications are designed to meet, and footnotes them directly to 'ILO et al. (2004), paragraph 3.144' — i.e. the Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice, predecessor of the current CPI Manual: Concepts and Methods. The Reference Paper's bibliography lists the manual in full: 'International Labour Office. 2004. Consumer Price Index Manual: Theory and Practice. Geneva.' This is StatCan sourcing a design rule of the Canadian CPI to the international manual, not merely listing it.

The QCEW Overview, under 'Industry Classification', states: 'QCEW currently uses the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) to classify industries for establishments.' QCEW publishes down to the 6-digit NAICS industry level and aggregates up through NAICS industry groups, sectors and supersectors, so the classification is the publication structure of the release, not an incidental reference.

The Statistics Canada survey record for Gross Domestic Product by Industry - National (Monthly), record no. 1301, states: 'The production estimates are published for 198 separate industries and 89 aggregates to provide a variety of levels of detail useful for analysis of industrial economic performance, using the North American Industrial Classification System.' The same record lists 'North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) Canada 2017 Version 3.0' among its formal documentation.

The Methodological Guide: Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts (catalogue 13-607-X) states: 'The CSMA is built using three main international macroeconomic accounting frameworks... The "Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual, Sixth Edition" is the underlying framework used to compile Canada's Balance of Payments and International Investment Position.' The guide adds that using these internationally adopted manuals 'ensures the resulting statistics are consistent and comparable with macroeconomic accounts compiled in the United States, Australia, the European Union and other countries.'

The same passage of the Methodological Guide: Canadian System of Macroeconomic Accounts names the third of the three frameworks: 'The "Government Finance Statistics Manual" is the underlying framework used to compile Canada's Government Finance Statistics.' Canadian Government Finance Statistics is one of the seven account categories that make up the CSMA.

On 5 May 2020 PSAB approved 'Option 2 - Adapt IPSAS principles when developing future standards' as its International Strategy: PSAB continues to issue Canadian Public Sector Accounting Standards, but future standards are based on the principles in the corresponding IPSAS, and PSAB will only amend an IPSAS principle where it is contrary to PSAB's own Conceptual Framework. PSAB has separately proposed modifying the Canadian public sector GAAP hierarchy in Section PS 1150 to position IPSAS as the go-to framework where PSAB has not issued a specific standard.

Painting a Portrait of Canada: The 2021 Census of Population (StatCan catalogue 98-26-0001) states: 'The need for internationally comparable information means that the census aims to comply with international standards set at global and regional levels. The United Nations reviews and sets census recommendations and principles every 10 years to ensure international consistency.' It adds that under the revised Statistics Act 'the census will follow the highest international standards'. Caveat: StatCan describes the UN standard by its function and revision cycle rather than naming Principles and Recommendations for Population and Housing Censuses by title.

The Guide to the Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours (catalogue 72-203-G) states: 'Each establishment is assigned an industry code according to the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) 2022 Version 1.0.' The dependency is load-bearing enough that NAICS revisions force revisions of the statistics themselves — the guide notes that adopting NAICS 2022 required a historical revision of SEPH estimates back to 2001, and that businesses which cannot be assigned a NAICS code are excluded from all variables except employment.

The BLS Handbook of Methods chapter on Current Employment Statistics - National, the payroll survey behind the Employment Situation release, states that all CES-N data on employment, hours and earnings are classified in accordance with the 2022 North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), as specified by the U.S. Office of Management and Budget. The industry detail published in the Employment Situation is NAICS detail.

The Guide to the Labour Force Survey (catalogue 71-543-G) defines the Industry variable as the 'General nature of the business carried out in the establishment where the person worked (main job only), based on the 2022 North American Industry Classification System (NAICS)', and states that in processing, 'industry, occupation and class of worker codes are assigned... based on the classifications described in the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) 2022 V1.0 and the National Occupational Classification (NOC) 2021 V1.0 standards.'

_dropped.why: The Canadian CPI does not use COICOP. Chapter 4 of the CPI Reference Paper describes a StatCan-specific hierarchy of roughly 700 elementary product classes rolling up to eight major aggregates (Food; Shelter; Household operations and furnishings; Clothing and footwear; Transportation; Health and personal care; Recreation, education and reading; Alcoholic beverages, tobacco products and recreational cannabis). COICOP is never named.

Explicitly denied by BLS. The Handbook of Methods CPI Concepts page states the CPI item structure 'is unique to the CPI and the categories themselves do not correspond to the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), other price indexes, or other statistics.' A documented non-dependency.

Searched hard and did not find it. The BLS Handbook of Methods CPI chapters (Overview, Concepts, Data sources, Design, Calculation, More Info) never cite the ILO/IMF Consumer Price Index Manual; the Concepts chapter grounds the CPI in the cost-of-living-index framework and cites no international manual at all. The only BLS documents that reference the manual are OSMR research working papers, which are not methodology statements for the release. So the CPI Manual sits under statcan-cpi but not under bls-cpi — an asymmetry, not an oversight.

Canada adheres to the IMF Special Data Dissemination Standard Plus and StatCan publishes Canada's National Summary Data Page as catalogue 13-608-X, so the relationship is real: SDDS Plus prescribes coverage, periodicity, timeliness and advance release calendars for these categories. But every document that states the obligation is IMF-side (the Dissemination Standards Bulletin Board DQAF pages, IMF press release 17/127). No StatCan methodology or release-schedule document was found saying that a given release's content or timing is governed by the SDDS. Dropped for want of national-side evidence, and because the only clean anchor would be a new StatCan node (the NSDP) with no other connections.

The direction of the documented relationship is backwards. BLS does not state that CPS employment and unemployment concepts follow the ICLS resolutions; its International Labor Comparisons methodology instead adjusts foreign countries' data 'as closely as possible to U.S. definitions'. Contrast StatCan's LFS guide, which does say its concepts 'are based on those endorsed by the International Labour Organization' — hence that edge exists in the graph and this one does not.

BEA's International Transactions Accounts are compiled on a BPM6 basis, but bea-gdp is the NIPA release, and no BEA document ties the headline GDP estimate to BPM6. Making this edge honest would require a separate BEA international accounts node, which is outside this slice.

PSAB's International Strategy points at IPSAS, not IFRS. IFRS reaches Canadian entities through the Accounting Standards Board and applies to publicly accountable enterprises rather than governments, and no node in the graph is governed by it. Included in the brief but not supportable as an edge onto psab-psas.

Removed on review, on the researching agent's own flag. BLS does publish an R-COICOP series monthly for the OECD, but it is a research series and an alternative aggregation — COICOP does not structure the headline CPI. The graph's edges describe what a release actually rests on, not every classification an agency also maps to. The COICOP node went with it, since that was its only edge. It should return if a document is found where COICOP governs a primary release.
